summary: DP is recursion with the repeated work cached. The method is always the same four steps: define the state (what actually varies), write the transition (how a state is built from smaller ones), pin the base cases, then memoise. Top-down memo is the safe default because it mirrors the recursion you already wrote; convert to bottom-up only when you need the space optimisation or want to drop the call stack. Most of Section 4 is one of three shapes: linear 1-D (stairs, min squares), grid/2-D (paths, max sum), or knapsack (pick-or-skip on index plus capacity).

thoughtProcess.title: 1. State first: what actually varies down the recursion?
thoughtProcess.body: Write the brute-force recursion, then look at its parameters. Whatever changes is the state; whatever is constant (the arrays, MOD, N) is not and must not enter the memo key. Getting this wrong is the single biggest source of wrong DP -- an under-specified state silently returns a cached answer computed under different conditions.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. Memo dimensions = the product of the state ranges.
thoughtProcess.body: State (index, capacity) -> int[N + 1][C + 1]. State (pos, sum) -> int[pos][sum + 1]. Size each dimension to max + 1 so the largest legal value is addressable. Time is then O(states * work per state), which is usually O(states) for an O(1) transition.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. The memo sentinel must be a value the answer can never take.
thoughtProcess.body: -1 is the usual choice, but it is WRONG when the answer can legitimately be -1 or when 0 means 'not computed' for a counting problem whose real answer is 0. Use Arrays.fill with -1 and make sure 0 is a valid cached result, or use Integer.MIN_VALUE for maximisation problems that can go negative.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. Pick-or-skip is 0/1; pick-and-stay is unbounded.
thoughtProcess.body: 0/1 knapsack: taking item i moves you to index i+1 (each item once). Unbounded: taking item i keeps you AT index i (unlimited copies). That one index difference is the whole distinction -- everything else about the two recursions is identical.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Grid DP: the answer at (i, j) comes from its predecessors, not its successors.
thoughtProcess.body: Decide direction once and keep it. Going from (1,1) to (n,m) moving right/down means dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]. Obstacles zero the cell out BEFORE the transition reads it. Base case is the start cell, and an obstacle sitting on the start or end makes the answer 0.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Convert to bottom-up only for a reason.
thoughtProcess.body: Top-down costs an O(depth) call stack but writes itself from the recursion. Go bottom-up when the depth risks a StackOverflow, or when row i only depends on row i-1 and you can roll a 2-D table into two 1-D arrays (or one, iterated backwards for 0/1 knapsack). Do not rewrite for style alone.

keyPatterns.name: Top-down memo skeleton
keyPatterns.when: Always start here once you have a working brute-force recursion.

keyPatterns.name: 0/1 knapsack (pick or skip, each item once)
keyPatterns.when: Choose a subset under a capacity limit, maximising value.

keyPatterns.name: Unbounded knapsack (unlimited copies)
keyPatterns.when: Same as 0/1 but each item may be reused any number of times.

keyPatterns.name: Grid paths with obstacles
keyPatterns.when: Count paths / min cost on a 2-D grid with blocked cells.

keyPatterns.name: Linear 1-D DP (take one step back, or a few)
keyPatterns.when: dp[i] depends on a fixed window of earlier indices.

keyPatterns.name: Two-state counting DP (position + running aggregate)
keyPatterns.when: Count sequences constrained by a running sum / digit / parity.
examples: N-digit Numbers with Digit Sum S

keyPatterns.name: Space-rolled bottom-up (2-D collapsed to 1-D)
keyPatterns.when: Row i depends only on row i-1 and you need O(C) space.

keyPatterns.name: Count-ways vs minimise-coins (same shape, different fold)
keyPatterns.when: Coin problems -- read carefully which one is being asked.

commonMistakes.title: Memo keyed on too few dimensions
commonMistakes.wrong:
int[] memo = new int[n];
// but the recursion is solve(index, capacity)
commonMistakes.why: Two different capacities at the same index share one slot, so the second call returns the first call's answer. The result is wrong but plausible-looking, which makes it very hard to spot. The memo key must contain every parameter that varies.

commonMistakes.title: Sentinel -1 when -1 (or 0) is a real answer
commonMistakes.wrong:
Arrays.fill(memo, -1);
if (memo[n] != -1) { return memo[n]; }   // but the answer can be -1
commonMistakes.right:
Arrays.fill(memo, Integer.MIN_VALUE);
if (memo[n] != Integer.MIN_VALUE) { return memo[n]; }
commonMistakes.why: A legitimately-cached -1 is re-treated as 'not computed', so that state recomputes forever and the memo stops working -- you silently fall back to exponential time and TLE.

commonMistakes.title: Storing into the memo after returning
commonMistakes.wrong: return Math.max(pick, skip);   // never written to memo
commonMistakes.why: The recursion is still correct but nothing is ever cached, so it runs at brute-force complexity. The symptom is TLE on large inputs with correct answers on small ones.

commonMistakes.title: 0/1 knapsack that recurses on the same index after picking
commonMistakes.wrong: pick = values[i] + knapsack(cap - weights[i], i, memo);
commonMistakes.right: pick = values[i] + knapsack(cap - weights[i], i + 1, memo);
commonMistakes.why: Staying at i lets the same item be taken repeatedly -- that is unbounded knapsack. One character separates the two problems, and the wrong one over-counts.

commonMistakes.title: Rolling the 1-D knapsack array forwards for 0/1
commonMistakes.wrong: for (int c = weights[i]; c <= cap; c++) { dp[c] = max(dp[c], v[i] + dp[c - w[i]]); }
commonMistakes.right: for (int c = cap; c >= weights[i]; c--) { dp[c] = max(dp[c], v[i] + dp[c - w[i]]); }
commonMistakes.why: Iterating forwards reads dp[c - w[i]] that was ALREADY updated for item i in this same pass, so item i gets reused -- you silently compute unbounded knapsack. Backwards keeps the read on the previous row.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting % MOD on intermediate sums
commonMistakes.wrong:
total = total + count(pos - 1, sum - d, memo);
return total % MOD;
commonMistakes.right: total = (total + count(pos - 1, sum - d, memo)) % MOD;
commonMistakes.why: The accumulator overflows int before the final modulo ever runs, so the modulo is applied to an already-wrapped negative number. Take the modulo at every addition, not once at the end.

commonMistakes.title: Obstacle check placed after the base case
commonMistakes.why: An obstacle sitting on the start cell must yield 0, not 1. The blocked-cell test has to run before any 'we arrived' test.

commonMistakes.title: Memo array allocated inside the recursive helper
commonMistakes.why: A memo re-allocated per call caches nothing. Allocate once in the public entry method and thread it through every recursive call.

edgeCases: N = 0 or an empty array -- return the identity (0 for sums/max, 1 for 'number of ways to make nothing').
Capacity 0 in knapsack: answer is 0, and the recursion must terminate before indexing weights.
An obstacle on the start or the destination cell makes the unique-paths answer 0.
A 1x1 grid: exactly one path (the empty path) unless that single cell is blocked.
Counting answers that are legitimately 0 -- make sure 0 is distinguishable from 'not yet computed'.
Answers that exceed int: use long for the accumulator, or apply % MOD at every step.
Unreachable states in a minimisation DP: represent them as Integer.MAX_VALUE and guard before doing 1 + sub.
Recursion depth near 1e5 will StackOverflow -- switch to bottom-up.
Coin denominations larger than the target: they must be skippable without indexing out of range.
Duplicate items in 0/1 knapsack are distinct items, not one reusable item.
